props.intro: We only run routes our guides have walked more than fifty times. Prices include flights to Lukla where needed, permits, guide, porter, rooms and all meals on the trail.

items.title: Everest Base Camp
items.text: Lukla, Namche, Tengboche and Kala Patthar at dawn. Two acclimatisation days, never rushed.

image.alt: The turquoise Gokyo lakes beside the Ngozumpa glacier

items.title: Gokyo Lakes
items.text: Quieter than Base Camp, with five turquoise lakes and a view of four 8,000-metre peaks from Gokyo Ri.

image.alt: A group of trekkers crossing glacier moraine

items.title: Three Passes
items.text: Kongma La, Cho La and Renjo La in one loop. For fit walkers with a trek or two behind them.

items.title: Langtang Valley
items.text: A jeep ride from Kathmandu, then yak pastures, cheese factories and Kyanjin Ri. No flights to cancel.

props.quote: My father carried loads to Base Camp for thirty years and never once was asked his name. Every porter who walks with us is paid first, insured, and introduced on day one.
props.name: Pasang Nuru Sherpa

props.heading: In every trek

items.title: Porters, paid properly
items.text: One porter for every two trekkers, carrying no more than 20 kilos, with boots, a jacket and insurance.

items.title: Rooms and three meals
items.text: Teahouse rooms with two beds, and whatever you want from the menu at breakfast, lunch and dinner.

items.text: Kathmandu to Lukla and back, the national park fee and the local area permit.

items.title: Twice-daily checks
items.text: Pulse and blood oxygen every morning and evening above 3,500 metres, written in a log.

items.title: A plan for bad days

props.heading: A day on the trail
props.intro: Most days are five to six hours of walking, with long stops.

image.alt: Trekkers resting on rocks facing Ama Dablam

items.title: Tea at your door
items.text: Your guide knocks with a cup of tea and asks how you slept. Porters are already packing.

items.title: Walk in the cold, clear morning
items.text: The best light and the best views are before ten. We walk at the pace of the slowest person, and nobody minds.

items.title: Lunch at a teahouse
items.text: Dal bhat, Sherpa stew or noodle soup. An hour to eat, sit in the sun and refill bottles.

items.title: Arrive, rest, walk high
items.text: On acclimatisation days we climb 300 metres after lunch and sleep low. Dinner by the yak-dung stove at six.

props.heading: Last season, from the trail
props.intro: Photographs from our guides’ phones and our guests’ cameras.

items.q: How fit do I need to be?
items.a: If you can walk six hours with a light pack on two days in a row, you can do Base Camp or Langtang. Three Passes needs more: steep, icy ground and long days.

items.q: What if the Lukla flight is cancelled?
items.a: It happens in cloud. Every Everest trek has one spare day. If we lose more, we move you by helicopter, shared with others, at cost, or rearrange the trek.
Yes, one that covers trekking to 5,600 metres and helicopter evacuation. We check it at the briefing.

items.q: Can we go privately, just the two of us?
items.a: Yes, on any date. A private trek costs about 15% more than a group place.

props.title: Everest in October, or Langtang in April?
props.text: Tell us when you can travel and how much walking you have done. Pasang answers every first message himself.

pages.title: Everest Base Camp
pages.seoTitle: Everest Base Camp trek, 14 days, day by day, from US$ 1,590
pages.seoDescription: Our 14-day Everest Base Camp itinerary with two acclimatisation days, Kala Patthar at sunrise, teahouses we trust and a spare day for Lukla weather.

props.title: Everest Base Camp in fourteen unhurried days
props.text: Two nights in Namche, one in Dingboche, sunrise from Kala Patthar and a spare day for the Lukla weather.

image.alt: The Everest Base Camp rock with prayer flags and the Khumbu icefall

props.eyebrow: Highest point 5,545 m · Moderate · From US$ 1,590

props.heading: Why fourteen days, not twelve
props.body:
Most people who turn back on the way to Base Camp do so because they climbed too fast, not because they were unfit. Above 3,000 metres we never sleep more than 500 metres higher than the night before, and we add a rest day at Namche and at Dingboche.

The extra two days cost less than one night in a Kathmandu hotel waiting for a flight home after altitude sickness.

items.title: Fly to Lukla, walk to Phakding
items.text: A 35-minute flight at dawn, then three hours downhill along the Dudh Koshi. 2,610 m.

items.title: To Namche Bazaar
items.text: Across the Hillary bridge and a long climb to the Sherpa capital. 3,440 m.

items.title: Rest in Namche
items.text: Walk up to the Everest View hotel ridge for the first sight of Everest, then back down to sleep.

items.title: To Tengboche
items.text: The monastery, and evening prayers if you are quiet. 3,860 m.

items.title: To Dingboche
items.text: Through Pangboche, past the tree line. 4,410 m.

items.title: Rest in Dingboche
items.text: Climb Nangkartshang for views of Makalu, and sleep low.

items.title: Lobuche, then Gorak Shep and Base Camp
items.text: Past the climbers’ memorials, then out along the glacier to Base Camp in the afternoon. 5,364 m.

items.title: Kala Patthar at sunrise
items.text: Two hours up in the dark for the best view of Everest there is. 5,545 m. Then down to Pheriche.

items.title: Back to Lukla
items.text: Downhill through Namche, with a night in each teahouse you liked on the way up.

items.title: Fly to Kathmandu, and a spare day
items.text: For the weather. If we do not need it, it is yours in the city.

image.alt: The painted gate of Tengboche monastery with snow peaks behind

props.caption: Tengboche, day 4. Evening puja starts at three; guides will take you in.

items.a: Early October to late November for clear skies, and March to May for rhododendrons and warmer nights. Winter is possible and very quiet, but cold.
At Gorak Shep in November, about minus 12 at night. We lend four-season sleeping bags and down jackets at no charge.
In every teahouse, for a fee. Bring a power bank for the cold nights; batteries drain fast.

pages.title: Guides and safety
pages.seoTitle: Our guides, porters and how we keep you safe at altitude
pages.seoDescription: Licensed Sherpa and Tamang guides with first-aid training, porters paid and insured, daily oxygen checks and a clear plan for altitude sickness.

props.title: The people who walk with you
props.text: Six guides and fourteen porters, most of them from the valleys we trek in. They work for us every season, not just when we are busy.

image.alt: A porter crossing a steel suspension bridge with a load

props.heading: Our guides
props.intro: Every guide holds a Nepal trekking guide licence and a wilderness first-aid certificate.

props.heading: If someone feels the altitude
props.intro: The same four steps on every trek, written in each guide’s notebook.

items.title: Stop and check
items.text: Pulse, oxygen level, and the Lake Louise questions. Written in the log.

items.title: Rest a day, no higher
items.text: Mild headache and nausea usually pass with a day at the same height, water and rest.

items.title: Go down
items.text: If it gets worse, we walk down at least 500 metres, day or night, with the guide.

items.title: Evacuate
items.text: If walking down is not enough, we call a helicopter through your insurer. We have done this four times in twelve years.

props.heading: How we treat porters
props.body:
Porters carry at most 20 kilos, including their own things. They get the same insurance as our guides, a proper jacket, boots and sunglasses, and a bed indoors every night.

They are paid in Kathmandu before the trek starts, not at the end. If a porter falls ill, the trek waits or we send someone down with him.

props.heading: What we carry on every trek

items.title: Pulse oximeter and log book
items.text: Checked morning and evening above 3,500 metres.

items.title: First-aid kit
items.text: Including acetazolamide, dexamethasone and blister care.

items.title: Satellite messenger
items.text: For places with no phone signal, on Three Passes and in upper Langtang.

items.title: Spare down jacket and bag
items.text: Because somebody always underpacks.
